name.text: Formulating proportional and capacity constraints for an organic mixture

questiontext.text:
A group of women farmers in Makueni managing a climate-resilient greenhouse project needs to prepare a liquid organic foliar feed mixture. They combine concentrated neem extract liquid (\(x\) liters) with an aloe vera solution base (\(y\) liters).

  • The mixing tank has a maximum storage capacity of {@C@} liters.
  • To guarantee effective pest control efficacy, the volume of neem extract liquid (\(x\)) must be at least {@R@} times the volume of the aloe vera solution base (\(y\)).

a) Write the linear inequalities that model the physical capacity and the chemical proportion limitations. (Use \( \le \) or \( \ge \) as appropriate. Do not include the non-negativity constraints \(x \ge 0, y \ge 0\)).

Tank capacity constraint: [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

Mixture proportion constraint: [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

b) The farmers decide to pour exactly {@y_val@} liters of aloe vera solution (\(y\)) into the mixing tank.

Based on your established inequalities, determine the allowable range for the neem extract (\(x\)):

1. What is the absolute minimum volume of neem extract required to satisfy the pest control efficacy proportion?

Minimum neem: [[input:ans3]] liters [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]

2. What is the absolute maximum volume of neem extract they can add without overflowing the mixing tank?

Maximum neem: [[input:ans4]] liters [[validation:ans4]] [[feedback:prt4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution:

Part a: Formulating the Constraints

1. Tank Capacity Constraint: The sum of both liquids cannot exceed the maximum volumetric size of the container. "Maximum capacity" implies less than or equal to (\(\le\)):

\( \displaystyle \boxed{{@ta1@}} \)

2. Mixture Proportion Constraint: The volume of neem (\(x\)) must be greater than or equal to \({@R@}\) times the aloe vera volume (\(y\)):

\( \displaystyle \boxed{{@ta2@}} \)

(Note: This can also be correctly rearranged and written as \( x - {@R*y@} \ge 0 \)).

Part b: Evaluating Operational Limits

We are given that \( y = {@y_val@} \). We must substitute this value into both inequalities to find the lower and upper bounds for \(x\).

1. Finding the Minimum (Efficacy Constraint):
Substitute \( y = {@y_val@} \) into \( x \ge {@R*y@} \):

\( \displaystyle \begin{aligned} x &\ge {@ta3@} \end{aligned} \)

The absolute minimum amount of neem extract required is {@ta3@} liters.

2. Finding the Maximum (Capacity Constraint):
Substitute \( y = {@y_val@} \) into \( x + y \le {@C@} \):

\( \displaystyle \begin{aligned} x + {@y_val@} &\le {@C@} \\ x &\le {@C@} - {@y_val@} \\ x &\le {@ta4@} \end{aligned} \)

The absolute maximum amount of neem extract that will safely fit is {@ta4@} liters.

Therefore, when using {@y_val@} liters of aloe vera, the farmers must add between {@ta3@} and {@ta4@} liters of neem extract to run a successful operation.

The graph shows both conditions; the shaded region holds every mixture that fits in the tank with enough neem.

questiondescription.text:
This question is based on the example of Ben's maize and beans (forming constraints from a situation) in the section Inequalities in Real Life of the CBC Grade 11 Mathematics textbook (INNODEMS).

Inequalities in Real Life (Proportions and Limits)

truefeedback.text: Correct constraint. "Maximum storage capacity" limits the total sum to be less than or equal to \({@C@}\).

node.description: Check if they used a strict inequality

truefeedback.text: The tank capacity is a maximum limit, which means the volume can perfectly equal the capacity without failing. You must use the inclusive \(\le\) symbol.

node.description: Check if they flipped the symbol

truefeedback.text: Check your inequality symbol. A capacity constraint requires the total volume to be smaller than the limit, not larger.

falsefeedback.text: Incorrect capacity constraint. Ensure you are adding the two volumes together (\(x + y\)) and limiting them by the tank's maximum size.

truefeedback.text: Correct constraint. The volume of \(x\) correctly scales to at least \({@R@}\) times the volume of \(y\).

node.description: Check if they used a strict inequality

truefeedback.text: The requirement is "at least", meaning the ratio can perfectly equal \({@R@}\). Use the inclusive \(\ge\) symbol.

node.description: Check if they flipped the symbol

truefeedback.text: Check your inequality symbol. Neem (\(x\)) must be the larger quantity relative to the scaled amount of aloe vera, so the symbol should point towards \(x\).

falsefeedback.text: Incorrect proportion constraint. Ensure you are directly relating the variable \(x\) to the multiplier \({@R@}\) applied to \(y\).

node.description: Check absolute correctness of minimum calculation

falsefeedback.text: Incorrect. Substitute \(y = {@y_val@}\) directly into your proportion constraint inequality to find the lowest acceptable boundary for \(x\).

node.description: Check absolute correctness of maximum calculation

falsefeedback.text: Incorrect. Substitute \(y = {@y_val@}\) directly into your tank capacity inequality to find the absolute physical limit for \(x\).
